extracted.intended_audience: public administrators, administrative analysts, and students of public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing organizational structures and administrative procedures in public agencies, including how to choose degrees of centralization, allocate line vs. staff functions, and shape administrative sequences. Emphasizes tradeoffs (control vs. speed/cost/duplication) and practical rules for adapting organization to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of concentration versus devolution of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance between concentration (centralization) and devolution (decentralization) of administrative power — central authorities seeking greater control vs. subordinates seeking minimum interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains effects: concentration transfers planning/control upward and can reduce subordinate executives to clerks; over-concentration burdens central officials with reports/requests; extreme devolution leads to duplication and conflict. The history of agencies shows pendulum swings between these extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust centralization to case-specific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no ‘one best’ degree of concentration of authority which will fit all organizations.” The proper adjustment depends on factors including the nature of the work, the environment (physical, political, legal, socio-psychological), the caliber of personnel, and mutual feelings between officials and subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contextual judgment (examples: high distrust or political tenseness argues for centralization; mutual confidence permits wide decentralization—as in British Colonial Service or American Forest/Indian services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer devolution when in doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts 'had better err in the direction of devolution, since it is easier to set up controls than to remove them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: decentralize where possible because adding controls later is easier than removing entrenched controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit control steps to situations where higher officials add value
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration (control/clearance steps) is warranted when higher officials can make a positive contribution to the administrative process; otherwise it produces useless red tape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a grant-in-aid sequence some numbered steps are only clerical/formal and could be dispensed with (numbers 4,5,8), while other steps (7 and 10) represent substantial review that probably improves the end-result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize unnecessary administrative moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration of authority tends to increase the number of moves in administrative sequences; devolution reduces them. Manage procedures so higher officials are consulted on important cases but not overwhelmed by minor matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by a case where adding normal control steps increased moves from five to twelve. Recommendation: cut out control steps in repeated sequences; allow direct communication for regularly interacting units provided superior officers are informed of matters meriting attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate line vs. staff functions clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish line functions (direct operations concerned with purposes/products/people outside the organization) from staff functions (providing ways and means, administrative processes, methods, organization, procedure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide for each intersection of a line function with a staff function whether the activity should be handled by the line or by a staff unit; the decision affects authority, routing, and control steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff units must justify their creation by net improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating staff divisions can justify themselves only by proving that their specialists can do their share of the work better — sufficiently so to compensate for additional administrative moves caused by shifting sequences to staff units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criterion: the end-result (considering performance of the operation and of the entire administrative job) must show improved quality and speed and a reduction in administrative cost. Solve line-vs-staff questions for each specific situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-elaboration of staff organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessively elaborate staff organization may impede line officers by making it impossible to act without reference to someone else and by introducing complications and delays into otherwise simple tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for the tradeoff: professionalization of staff functions lightens line load but increases administrative moves; do not centralize to the point that it paralyzes routine action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent staff agencies from becoming autonomous control agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff agencies risk becoming control agencies that intervene in line functions in light of what they believe to be executive policy; such active staff must be restrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options for control: require staff instructions be issued over a line administrator's signature to preserve scalar fiction, or accept divergent delegation and allow staff to issue instructions on their own responsibility. Maintain checks so staff do not overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider functionalism cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionalism argues for organizing entirely by staff/process functions so a single unit performs each process for the whole organization (centralizing stenography, filing, drafting, planning, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionalism can improve performance and avoid wasted time from slack work, but centralizing overlapping processes may remove duties from line units and should be weighed against the cost of added administrative moves and loss of line responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tighter control for new or radical agencies to secure unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: New agencies or those carrying out radical programs require tighter control to secure unity of action; older, uncontroversial organizations can often operate on a decentralized basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: adopt more centralization when agency mission is novel/controversial or when unity is essential; relax controls for stable, established agencies with low controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design channels of contact to reflect desired degree of concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: If channels of contact are drawn on an organization chart, more concentration implies more vertical lines (communications routed through superiors); more devolution implies more horizontal/oblique lines (direct unit-to-unit contact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal: ensure higher officials are consulted on important matters while avoiding needless routing of routine exchanges through central offices; allow 'blanket' clearance or delegated direct contacts where appropriate.
